The Team
Who We Are
⚙️We engineer solutions, not just robots.
💡Building the future, one match at a time.
🏆Excited for our rookie season in V5RC as Team 91276C — same ninjas, bigger stage.

We build robots—and the skills to understand them.

Robotex Ninjas is a North Texas student robotics team within Ninjas STEM Foundation. Through student-led projects and adult mentorship, we develop skills in mechanical design, programming, testing, technical documentation, and teamwork.

Competitions give us opportunities to evaluate our work, learn from other teams, and improve our designs. Workshops and demonstrations give us opportunities to share what we learn with other students.

Explore our engineering projects, community activities, and participation opportunities below.

Tech Spotlight

Cool technology worth knowing about — summarized by the team, with thoughts from our members on what it means for the future.

AI • Game Design • Google I/O
Google Built Five Playable Games With Gemini — And Let Anyone Remix the Code
Google Blog  •  Mar 2026  •  blog.google ↗
⌄
🎮 What it is

Ahead of Google I/O 2026, Google's developer team built a “Save the Date” countdown puzzle out of five playable mini-games, all built with their Gemini AI model. The lineup includes Supersonic Bot, a side-scroller you steer by how loud you talk into your microphone; Hole in One, a mini-golf game with an AI caddy that gives you tips based on your actual shots; and Nonogram, a logic puzzle where the later levels are freshly generated by Gemini every time you play, so no two rounds are identical. Finish all five and you unlock Dino Pal, a virtual version of Chrome's offline dinosaur whose personality changes based on how you played.

🔧 What it's used for

It's a demo of two different things AI can do for games at once: showing up inside the gameplay itself (the AI caddy, the ever-changing puzzle levels), and doing the actual building behind the scenes — the team prototyped ideas in Google AI Studio and says a lot of the AI-generated code went straight into the shipped games. Google's stated goal was to make something “fun, challenging, creative and rewarding” for casual players and curious builders alike.

🚀 Why this matters for our team

Every one of these games is open to remix — the underlying code is viewable and editable in Google AI Studio, so you can see exactly how Gemini generated a new Nonogram puzzle or wrote the AI caddy's advice, then change it and make it your own. That's a genuinely approachable way to go from “playing a game” to “reading and tweaking real AI-assisted code,” which is exactly the kind of hands-on building our team already does with VEX — just in software instead of hardware.

💬 What our team thinks

AI • Companion Robots
ElliQ — The AI Companion Robot for Older Adults
Intuition Robotics  •  intuitionrobotics.com ↗
⌄
🔍 What it does

ElliQ is an AI-powered companion robot designed specifically for older adults who live alone. Built by Intuition Robotics, it sits on a table and proactively starts conversations, suggests light exercises, helps users stay connected with family, and monitors wellbeing — without waiting to be asked. It learns from every interaction, building memory of the person’s preferences, health goals, and emotional state over time. Real-world results show a 95% reduction in loneliness, 90% improvement in health and wellness, and 79% improvement in social connectedness among users.

🧠 What makes it interesting

ElliQ uses what Intuition Robotics calls a “Relationship Orchestrator” — a system that mimics how humans actually build relationships with each other. It tracks context from past conversations, reads emotional cues, uses voice, body language, lights, and sound together, and decides when to initiate an interaction based on the person’s availability and goals. It’s not just a chatbot on a screen. It’s designed to feel like a presence.

💬 What our team thinks
Luke  •  Driver & Coder

It’s interesting that the robot doesn’t just answer questions — it actually decides when to talk to you first. That’s exactly what autonomous behavior looks like in a real-world setting. In competition, we program our robot to make decisions without a driver. ElliQ does the same thing, just for people instead of game pieces.

MIT • App Development • AI for Kids
MIT App Inventor — Build Real AI-Powered Apps Without Writing a Single Line of Code
MIT CSAIL  •  Free  •  ai2a.appinventor.mit.edu ↗
⌄
📱 What it is

MIT App Inventor is a free, drag-and-drop visual programming environment built by MIT that lets anyone — even complete beginners — build fully functional apps for iPhone and Android. No typing code required. You snap together blocks like puzzle pieces to create logic, and your app runs on a real phone. A first app can be running in under 30 minutes. The AI2A version adds powerful AI capabilities — image recognition, text classification, chatbot integration, speech recognition, and more. It has produced over 100 million apps by more than 24 million learners across 195 countries.

💡 What skills it builds

App Inventor teaches you to think like a programmer — breaking problems into steps, designing interfaces, and building logic that responds to real events. Skills developed include computational thinking, UI/UX design, AI model training, problem-solving, and project management. These map directly to what top CS and AI programs look for.

🌟 Why it matters

Six middle-school girls from a small Texas border town used App Inventor to build a navigation app for their blind classmate — and were invited to present it at the White House. This tool turns kids from technology consumers into technology creators. With the AI features, you can build apps powered by the same kind of machine learning behind modern AI tools — just with blocks instead of code. It’s free. It works on any browser. There’s zero reason not to try it.

Robotics • Competition • Humanoid Robots
World Humanoid Robot Games 2026 — A Robot Beat Usain Bolt’s 100m Record, Then Couldn’t Hammer a Nail
Nature  •  Aug 2026  •  nature.com ↗
⌄
🏆 What happened

Beijing hosted the second annual World Humanoid Robot Games from August 22–26, 2026, drawing more than 600 competing teams — mostly Chinese universities, research institutes, and robotics companies — across dozens of sporting and “scenario-based” events. In the headline moment, a robot built by X-Humanoid won the 100-meter sprint in 8.64 seconds, almost a full second faster than Usain Bolt’s human world record of 9.58 seconds. Another robot broke the standing high jump record, clearing roughly 3.4 meters from a stand. Just one year earlier, the fastest robot at the very same event finished the 100m in 21.5 seconds — a jump in performance that shows how fast this field is moving.

🤖 The twist

The games also included real-world “scenario” events like shelving books, making beds, and hammering nails into a board — and here the robots struggled, even when a human was steering their hands by remote control. Researchers explain that sprinting and jumping are actually easier for robots than everyday chores, because those athletic movements follow a fixed, pre-planned path the robot can execute perfectly, step by step, without needing to think or adapt. Folding laundry or gripping a hammer requires constant improvising and fine finger control — a far harder problem for today’s robotic hands. As one Stanford robotics researcher put it, for a humanoid a daily task like folding laundry is actually harder than doing a backflip.

🚀 Why this matters for our team

This is basically VEX competition logic playing out on a world stage. The Games score autonomous performance separately from human-operated performance — robots that complete a task entirely on their own earn full points, while robots that are teleoperated by a human hand only earn partial credit for the same task. That’s the exact same principle behind the autonomous period in our own VEX matches: a robot that can sense, decide, and act without a driver is worth more than one that needs a human at the controls the whole time. It’s also a reminder that the skills we already practice — coding autonomous routines, mechanical design for dexterity, testing under real constraints — are the same frontier the biggest robotics companies in the world are racing to solve right now.

💬 What our team thinks

Google • Stanford • AI Literacy • Free • Ages 11–14
Google AI Quests — Become an AI Researcher. Save the World. No Code Required.
Google Research & Stanford  •  Launched Sept 2025  •  research.google/ai-quests ↗
⌄
🎮 What it is

Google AI Quests is a free, game-based learning platform built by Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning for students ages 11–14. You step into the role of an AI researcher guided by an in-game mentor called Professor Skye, and tackle real-world problems using actual Google AI. No coding. No prior experience. Just curiosity and a browser. The first quest is built on Google’s real flood forecasting technology — the same system currently sending flood warnings to communities worldwide. Future quests cover detecting diabetic eye disease and mapping the human brain neuron by neuron.

🤖 What you actually do

Each quest mirrors the real stages of an AI project. You define the problem, collect and evaluate data, train an AI model, and test it against real scenarios. You see directly how the decisions you make — which data to include, how to handle bad data — change what the AI does. Students are not just learning about AI. They are making decisions that a real AI researcher would make, using the same kind of data Google actually used.

🚀 How we can use it

For our team — AI Quests builds exactly the systems thinking and data intuition that makes better coders and robot builders. Understanding how training data shapes a model’s decisions is directly useful when programming autonomous routines. For STEM Academy workshops — it comes with complete lesson plans, requires zero teacher AI expertise, and works on any browser. We could run a full AI literacy session around one quest with zero setup. For the Innovation Lab — students building AI-powered science fair projects will understand the fundamentals far better after one quest. It’s free, built by Google and Stanford, and made for exactly our age group.

💬 What our team thinks
Luke  •  Driver & Coder
🌎 Quest: Predicting Floods
I collected data to help predict floods — rainfall, elevation, humidity and more. Then cleaned it by removing anything that didn’t look right, selected the most relevant variables to train the AI model, and trained it using flood scenarios from different locations around the world. The final step was placing emergency stalls in the safest locations based on the AI’s forecast.
😲 What surprised me

Nothing surprised me that much — but the fact that AI is essentially useless without humans taking the first steps was pretty interesting. AI can’t do anything if humans hadn’t first collected the data, evaluated it, and trained it. The machine needs us before we ever need it.

💡 What made me want to learn more

The fact that AI can be incredibly useful if used correctly — but could actually harm people if it’s not properly trained or built on inaccurate data. That tension between power and responsibility is something I want to understand better.

AI • Coding • Future Skills • Andrew Ng
Vibe Coding — Everyone Should Learn to Code with AI. Here’s Why.
Business Insider  •  Nov 2025  •  businessinsider.com ↗
⌄
💡 What is vibe coding?

Vibe coding is a new way of building software where instead of writing every line of code yourself, you describe what you want in plain language and let AI tools — like Cursor, Replit, or GitHub Copilot — generate the code for you. The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy, an OpenAI co-founder and former Tesla AI director, in early 2025. The idea: focus on high-level ideas and let the AI handle the implementation. Andrew Ng — founder of Google Brain and Stanford professor — says everyone should learn this skill, not just software engineers. “The bar to coding is now lower than it ever has been,” he said at Snowflake’s Build conference. “People that code, be it CEOs, marketers, recruiters — not just software engineers — will really get more done than those who don’t.”

⚠ But it’s not as easy as it sounds

Ng himself pushes back on the name. “It’s unfortunate that it’s called vibe coding,” he said — because the word “vibe” makes it sound like you just accept whatever the AI suggests. In reality, coding with AI “is a deeply intellectual exercise” that requires real thought, judgment, and oversight. Asking an AI to do everything in one shot “usually does not work.” The skill is knowing how to guide the AI, check its output, and course-correct when it goes wrong. That judgment — not just the typing — is what makes someone a good vibe coder.

🚀 Why this matters for our team

We already use AI tools in our robot programming. Understanding that AI-assisted coding is a real career skill — not a shortcut — changes how we should think about what we’re building. Ng warns that advice telling young people “don’t learn to code because AI will automate it” is “some of the worst career advice ever given.” The future isn’t humans vs. AI at the keyboard. It’s humans who know how to direct AI doing the work of ten. Job listings at Visa, Reddit, DoorDash and hundreds of startups now explicitly require vibe coding experience. This is already the job market.
